comment: I am exceedingly disappointed with the proceedings of the last council meeting on 9/1/22 where all of you approved the continuation of trail building on Bonanza Flat despite your own voiced concerns that you don't even understand the plans. After all our discussions and meetings, no changes have been made, and trail building is continuing despite my and my neighbors' concerns. Frankly I feel like I just got slapped in the face. Yes, we did save the property from being developed into a luxury neighborhood, but that doesn't mean we should turn it into a "recreation hub" - Utah Open Lands words to describe the property. Bike trails and recreation does not equal conservation. I am frankly tired of all the pats on the shoulder Utah Open Lands and trails staff are receiving for not doing the one job they were supposed to do - be good stewards of the property. Before the property was "saved" maybe, at most, 100 people a day visited it. Now 1000s of people visit a day. There is more trash, more dog poop, more damage now than there ever was before. How is this conservation? Bloods Lake and the rest of the property would have been better served by not having the new Bloods Lake Trailhead with a flat wide trail that makes it so very easy to get there. Twenty years ago it may have been enough to just save a property from development, but that is no loner enough. We need to be active stewards of land, protecting it from commercial development, and from too much love and too much recreation. We, as humans, can wield incredible power over the landscape and have the ability to save it from ourselves. If you continue to build trails without fully understanding the implications you will destroy this property. Please, please slow this development. Work with area stakeholders and do traffic and safety studies. Work to protect the wildlife, not push them out. A trail cut is a scar on the landscape. Once you make it, it will be there for many years. It is better to go slowly rather than unnecessarily cut down trees and damage the land. There are existing trails already that can be used to finish the "multi-use trail". There is no need to further scar the landscape. Please direct staff to slow down, write safety and traffic studies and utilize existing trails only.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I appreciated the opportunity to serve on the Transportation Committee. The final publication is impressive in its voluminous output of targeted projects, and Sarah, Alex and co have much to be proud of. However, I have a differing view on the overarching philosophy that "large-bus" park and rides on our entry corridors will solve our congestion beyond a short timeframe, or that they will integrate favorably with a convenient local transportation system to replace cars for local residents – whereas a system that delivers both and the holy grail of a single transit trip is possible, functional, useable and far more sustainable. This plan on its own supports growth more than it balances the needs of long-time residents. It’s a proven fact that Park and Rides do not solve traffic congestion. They offer temporary relief that ultimately fails without a corresponding or equal reduction in parking where people congregate – it’s metaphorically no different than adding another lane to the highway that induces more demand. We should all cringe when we hear the words “doing something is better than nothing” (Quinns), as it’s plainly untrue. There’s lots of real world examples that demonstrate this fact (I have been involved with some 40+ years ago in the UK, while ski towns in the US are beginning to experience this inevitability). The immediate deterrent of paid parking eventually fades over time (Old Town parking on Sundays?). Adding to Park City’s problem is the resort's controlling influence over parking that is less concerned with reducing congestion than it is about remaining competitive, and profitable. Residents should be a priority and they are not. Parking must be limited at the attractions, and expertly placed elsewhere, it’s not. Transit must be designed for everyone year round, it’s not. Core receiving zone(s) must have modernized concepts to replace cars with expertly designed usable and efficient localized transit systems, they do not. Streamlining/collaboration of amenity and service of multiple developments must be prioritized, they are not. Park City has an opportunity to capitalize on a once in a lifetime opportunity to expertly re-think and plan 3 of its 4 major hubs for the future it wants (bold change at PCMR, DV & BP). The concept and everlasting benefit of parking reduction at our core congestion zones is well known by planning staff who initially proposed a 20% reduction at the base of PCMR, that mysteriously disappeared without explanation (see resorts controlling influence above?). It’s incumbent on our political leaders to raise these issues and demand more integration between development and transportation planning to deliver the Park City we all strive for and the community visioning desires.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)
